{
  "measurements": [
    {
      "statistic": "concordance rate",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the rate of translation from animal to human studies.",
      "compared": "animal studies vs human studies",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "A scoping review performed as part of this project Ritskes-Hoitinga and Pound found that rates of translation from animal to human studies ranged from 0 to 100 and appeared to be random, with no indication of factors that might increase its likelihood.31"
    },
    {
      "statistic": "permissible studies",
      "value": 7,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the proportion of animal studies that were deemed permissible based on harm-benefit analysis.",
      "compared": "animal studies vs human benefits",
      "species": [],
      "n": 212,
      "n_counts": "animal studies",
      "verbatim": "Using Bateson’s Cube34 to weigh the harms to animals used in the research against the benefits to humans that resulted, and taking into account the importance and quality of the research studies, they concluded that fewer than 7% of the 212 animal studies scrutinised were permissible.35"
    },
    {
      "statistic": "positive findings",
      "value": 82,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the proportion of preclinical animal studies referenced in investigator brochures that reported positive findings.",
      "compared": "preclinical animal studies vs investigator brochures",
      "species": [],
      "n": 109,
      "n_counts": "investigator brochures",
      "verbatim": "A German study of 109 investigator brochures, the documents presented to ethics review boards by those applying to conduct Phase I and II trials in humans, revealed that only 6% of the preclinical animal studies referenced in the brochures reported an outcome demonstrating no effect; the vast majority – 82% – were described as reporting positive findings.14"
    },
    {
      "statistic": "no effect outcomes",
      "value": 6,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the proportion of preclinical animal studies referenced in investigator brochures that reported an outcome demonstrating no effect.",
      "compared": "preclinical animal studies vs investigator brochures",
      "species": [],
      "n": 109,
      "n_counts": "investigator brochures",
      "verbatim": "A German study of 109 investigator brochures, the documents presented to ethics review boards by those applying to conduct Phase I and II trials in humans, revealed that only 6% of the preclinical animal studies referenced in the brochures reported an outcome demonstrating no effect; the vast majority – 82% – were described as reporting positive findings.14"
    },
    {
      "statistic": "protocols needing amending",
      "value": 50,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the proportion of protocols for forthcoming animal experiments that needed amending to ensure proper experimental design, appropriate sample sizes, and measures to control bias.",
      "compared": "animal experiment protocols vs amended protocols",
      "species": [],
      "n": 255,
      "n_counts": "protocols for forthcoming animal experiments",
      "verbatim": "And when scientists from Astra Zeneca reviewed 255 protocols for forthcoming animal experiments, they found that over half needed amending to ensure proper experimental design, appropriate sample sizes and measures to control bias.15"
    },
    {
      "statistic": "studies showing no effect",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "the proportion of animal studies showing adverse effects that were omitted from the preclinical evidence.",
      "compared": "animal studies showing adverse effects vs omitted studies",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "The group had gained funding for the human trials, but the trials had ultimately failed. An earlier systematic review of the animal data concluded that insufficient evidence had existed to support claims about the efficacy of the vaccine booster and that the claims had been overstated.29 Highlighting the problem of selective outcome reporting, the BMJ commented on the group’s ‘pick and mix’ approach, claiming that some of the animal studies showing adverse effects had been omitted from the preclinical evidence."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "advocating focus on human-relevant research",
      "value": 1,
      "unit": "count",
      "measures": "the number of authors who advocated a focus on human-relevant research instead of animal models of stroke.",
      "compared": "authors' opinions on animal models of stroke vs human-relevant research",
      "species": [],
      "n": 80,
      "n_counts": "authors",
      "verbatim": "They found that while many viewed species differences as a significant problem in preclinical stroke research, the vast majority were reluctant to abandon their animal models, with only 1 of 80 authors advocating a focus on human-relevant research instead."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "votes to develop a coordinated plan to replace animal experiments",
      "value": 667,
      "unit": "count",
      "measures": "the number of votes in favor of developing a coordinated plan to replace animal experiments with innovative, non-animal methodologies.",
      "compared": "European Parliament votes vs plan to replace animal experiments",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "And in September 2021, the European Parliament voted by a stunning majority of 667 to 4 to develop a coordinated plan to replace animal experiments with innovative, non-animal methodologies.49,50"
    },
    {
      "statistic": "votes against developing a coordinated plan to replace animal experiments",
      "value": 4,
      "unit": "count",
      "measures": "the number of votes against developing a coordinated plan to replace animal experiments with innovative, non-animal methodologies.",
      "compared": "European Parliament votes vs plan to replace animal experiments",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "And in September 2021, the European Parliament voted by a stunning majority of 667 to 4 to develop a coordinated plan to replace animal experiments with innovative, non-animal methodologies.49,50"
    }
  ],
  "headline_index": null,
  "what_the_study_did": "This study reviews the evidence generated by systematic reviews of preclinical animal research to identify limitations and implications for preclinical research and medicine.",
  "what_it_found": "Systematic reviews have exposed significant shortcomings in the design, conduct, reporting, and translation of preclinical animal research, raising doubts about its robustness and clinical relevance.",
  "key_quotes": [
    {
      "quote": "As more and more animal studies were scrutinised as part of the systematic review process, it gradually became apparent that much animal research was conducted to a low standard and was therefore unable to generate robust, reliable data.",
      "topic": "Low standard research"
    },
    {
      "quote": "In short, systematic reviews provided overwhelming evidence that animal studies suffer from poor experimental design and a lack of scientific rigour, raising doubts about the robustness of their findings and consequently, their clinical relevance.",
      "topic": "Poor design and rigor"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Selective analysis and biased outcome reporting – the practice of reporting only the most positive outcomes and analyses from among the many performed and studied – was also revealed to be a problem in animal research.",
      "topic": "Biased reporting"
    },
    {
      "quote": "This problem – which has come to be known as the reproducibility crisis – is due to poor experimental design and poor scientific conduct and is compounded by incomplete reporting.",
      "topic": "Reproducibility crisis"
    },
    {
      "quote": "They noted that shortcomings in almost every aspect of the scientific design, conduct and reporting of animal studies were contributing to an inability to translate into benefits for humans.",
      "topic": "Inability to translate"
    },
    {
      "quote": "First, the inability of many, if not most animal models to replicate complex human diseases; and second, the problem of species differences.",
      "topic": "Model limitations"
    }
  ]
}
